title: Microsoft Copilot reveals secret input that allowed it to be hacked
gist: Varonis researchers got Microsoft 365 Copilot to disclose an undocumented ?autorun=1 parameter that bypassed user-consent guardrails, enabling a one-click attack ('Co-Snitch') that silently exfiltrates passwords and inbox data—underscoring that LLM security rests on brittle reactive guardrails rather than robust design.

insights.claim: Researchers extracted an undocumented Microsoft Copilot parameter (?autorun=1) simply by repeatedly asking the assistant about its own guardrails, then combined it with ?q= to silently execute prompts the moment a victim clicked a malicious URL.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Demonstrates LLMs can leak their own security-critical internals; an enterprise-security risk for the fast-spreading AI-assistant category.
insights.quote: Copilot eventually disclosed undocumented parameters. I took those parameters and used them for prompts for running automatically.

insights.claim: The one-click 'Co-Snitch' attack ran with full access to the victim's authenticated session, connected apps, and memory, completing even if the Copilot tab was closed, and exfiltrated base64-encoded data to an attacker server.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Shows agentic assistants with broad app access create high-impact single-click data-exfiltration surfaces for enterprises.
insights.locator: A Varonis blog post published Tuesday

insights.claim: A separate Varonis attack used prompt injection hidden in webpage metadata to poison Copilot's permanent memory store, with false memories persisting across password changes, session revocations, and device re-enrollments.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Persistent-memory features create durable compromise that standard remediation (password reset) cannot clear—a novel enterprise threat.

insights.claim: Microsoft silently mitigated the flaw in February and shipped fuller fixes, but the article argues LLM security is largely built on reactive restrictions ('guardrails') that frequently fail rather than proactive design.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The reactive-guardrail paradigm is a structural weakness across AI assistants—recurring vulnerability risk as enterprises deploy them widely.
insights.quote: LLM developers erect guardrails that they hope will minimize the harm when things go bad. These guardrails frequently fail
